newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar surges versus mark and yen after G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges versus mark and yen after G7 meeting.

text.p: The dollar surged against the yen and the mark in Tokyo on Monday after the Group of Seven (G7) failed to specifically refer to recent yen movements against the dollar in a statement at the end of its meeting in Washington, dealers said.

"The dollar started climbing after (Japanese Finance Minister) Mitsuzuka's remarks saying that the G7 statement would not specifically refer to the yen," said Wataru Ito, deputy general manager Sanwa Bank Ltd's treasury department.
Mitsuzuka told Reuters as he emerged from the G7 meeting that the communique did not make a specific reference to recent movements in the yen.

The G7 statement on currencies said: "We agreed that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility and significant deviations from fundamentals are undesirable. In this context, we emphasised the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances."

Sanwa Bank's Ito said: "The G7 meeting could have been considered somewhat of a turning point for the dollar/yen rally, but in fact, the lack of strong remarks on the yen will open the way for the dollar to rise to 130 yen."
Another city bank dealer said: "I did not see any comments that were stronger than those at the last G7 meeting in Berlin, so traders started buying dollars."
Ito said some traders had contracted to buy yen against the dollar, expecting the G7 to make a strong statement about the excessive decline in the yen.
The greenback rose as high as 127.10 yen in early Tokyo trading, which also helped push it up against the mark.
The dollar was quoted around 126.70/80 yen in early morning trade.
Dealers said the dollar jumped against the German currency on comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer after the G7 meeting that foreign exchange rates reflected economic fundamentals.
"All in all, I have the impression that rates are appropriate and reflect fundamentals," Tietmeyer said.

The greenback rose as high as 1.7395 marks in early trade, its highest level since February 1994, although it retreated modestly on later comments by Tietmeyer that the U.S. wanted a strong dollar but not a stronger dollar.
The market had not been fazed, however, by earlier comments by Tietmeyer that he could not go along with forecasts that the mark may fall to a yearly average of 1.80 marks to the dollar.

"His (latter) comments could mean that Germany will not be too worried about the dollar/mark level until it moves too close to 1.80 marks," the city bank dealer said, adding that the 1.74 mark level is not likely to be a major obstacle even though it has so far capped the dollar's recent rally.

In their joint communique, the central bank governors and finance ministers of the G7, comprising Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, also said its members will cooperate as appropriate in the foreign exchange markets.

Asked about the possibility of concerted intervention, Ito said: "Since there are different views about the dollar between Japan and European nations, it seems difficult for the G7 nations to conduct concerted intervention."
